The Preamble explains that the guidelines summarize and evaluate available evidence to assist health professionals in proposing the best management strategies for individual patients. They facilitate decision-making but are not a substitute for the patient–practitioner relationship. Final decisions must be made by responsible health professionals, in consultation with the patient and caregiver. The guidelines are freely available from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), represent the ESC’s official position, and are regularly updated. In addition to Clinical Practice Guidelines, the ESC conducts the EUROObservational Research Programme of registries to assess diagnostic and therapeutic practices based on high-quality routine clinical data, and develops quality indicators to evaluate guideline implementation.

recommendation_tables.title: Pre-operative assessment in patients with a newly detected murmur, chest pain, dyspnoea, or peripheral oedema

rows.recommendation: In patients with a newly detected murmur and symptoms or signs of CVD, TTE is recommended before NCS.
In patients with a newly detected murmur suggesting clinically significant pathology, TTE is recommended before high-risk NCS.
In patients with a newly detected murmur, but without other signs or symptoms of CVD, TTE should be considered before moderate and high-risk NCS.
If a patient scheduled for elective NCS has chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of undetected CAD, further diagnostic work-up before NCS is recommended.

If a patient in need of acute NCS also has chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of undetected CAD, a multidisciplinary assessment approach is recommended to choose the treatment with lowest total risk for the patient.
In patients with dyspnoea and/or peripheral oedema, an ECG and an NT-proBNP/BNP test is indicated before NCS, unless there is a certain non-cardiac explanation.
In patients with dyspnoea and/or peripheral oedema and elevated NT-proBNP/BNP, TTE is recommended before NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Patient information

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to give patients individualized instructions for pre-operative and post-operative changes in medication, in verbal and written formats with clear and concise directions.
It should be considered to set up a structured information list (e.g. a checklist to help with common issues) for patients with CVD or at high risk of CV complications scheduled for NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Pre-operative assessment tools—Section 4: Frailty and functional capacity

rows.recommendation: In patients aged ≥70 years, being scheduled to undergo intermediate- or high-risk NCS, frailty screening should be considered using a validated screening tool.
Adjusting risk assessments according to self-reported ability to climb two flights of stairs should be considered in patients referred for intermediate- or high-risk NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Pre-operative assessment tools—Section 4: Transthoracic echocardiography

rows.recommendation: TTE is recommended in patients with poor functional capacity and/or high NT-proBNP/BNP, or if murmurs are detected before high-risk NCS, in order to undertake risk-reduction strategies.
TTE should be considered in patients with suspected new CVD or unexplained signs or symptoms before high-risk NCS.
TTE may be considered in patients with poor functional capacity, abnormal ECG, high NT-proBNP/BNP, or ≥1 clinical risk factor before intermediate-risk NCS.
To avoid delaying surgery, a FOCUS exam performed by trained specialists may be considered as an alternative to TTE for pre-operative triage.

recommendation_tables.title: Pre-operative assessment tools—Section 4: Stress imaging

rows.recommendation: Stress imaging should be considered before high-risk NCS in asymptomatic patients with poor functional capacity, and previous PCI or CABG.

recommendation_tables.title: Coronary angiography

rows.recommendation: CCTA should be considered to rule out CAD in patients with suspected CCS or biomarker-negative NSTE-ACS in case of low-to-intermediate clinical likelihood of CAD, or in patients unsuitable for non-invasive functional testing undergoing non-urgent, intermediate-, and high-risk NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Cardiovascular risk factors and lifestyle interventions

rows.recommendation: Smoking cessation >4 weeks before NCS is recommended to reduce post-operative complications and mortality.
Control of CV risk factors—including blood pressure, dyslipidaemia, and diabetes—is recommended before NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Pharmacological treatment

rows.recommendation: For patients on diuretics to treat hypertension, transient discontinuation of diuretics on the day of NCS should be considered.
It should be considered to interrupt SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy for at least 3 days before intermediate- or high-risk NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Antiplatelets

rows.recommendation: For patients undergoing high bleeding risk surgery (e.g. intracranial, spinal neurosurgery, or vitreoretinal eye surgery), it is recommended to interrupt aspirin for at least 7 days pre-operatively.
In high-risk patients with a recent PCI (e.g. STEMI patients or high-risk NSTE-ACS patients), a DAPT duration of at least 3 months should be considered before time-sensitive NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Anticoagulants

rows.recommendation: When an urgent surgical intervention is required, it is recommended that NOAC therapy is immediately interrupted.
In non-minor bleeding risk procedures in patients using a NOAC, it is recommended to use an interruption regimen based on the NOAC compound, renal function, and bleeding risk.
In minor bleeding risk surgery and other procedures where bleeding can easily be controlled, it is recommended to perform surgery without interruption of OAC therapy.
In patients using NOACs, it is recommended that minor bleeding risk procedures are performed at trough levels (typically 12–24 h after last intake).
LMWH is recommended, as an alternative to UFH, for bridging in patients with MHVs and high surgical risk.

For patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valves undergoing NCS, bridging with UFH or LMWH should be considered if OAC interruption is needed and patients have: (i) mechanical AVR and any thromboembolic risk factor; (ii) old-generation mechanical AVR; or (iii) mechanical mitral or tricuspid valve replacement.
Idarucizumab should be considered in patients on dabigatran and requiring urgent surgical intervention with intermediate to high bleeding risk.
For interventions with a very high risk of bleeding, such as spinal or epidural anaesthesia, interruption of NOACs for up to five half-lives and re-initiation after 24 h should be considered.

rows.recommendation: When specific reversal agents are unavailable, PCC or activated PCC should be considered for reversing NOAC effects.

If an urgent surgical intervention is required, specific coagulation tests and assessment of NOAC plasma levels should be considered to interpret routine coagulation tests and waning of anticoagulant effect.

If bleeding risk with resumption of full-dose anticoagulation outweighs the risk of thromboembolic events, postponing therapeutic anticoagulation 48–72 h after the procedure may be considered, using post-operative thromboprophylaxis until resumption of full OAC dose is deemed safe.
Bridging of OAC therapy is not recommended in patients with low/moderate thrombotic risk undergoing NCS.
Use of reduced-dose NOAC to attenuate the risk of post-operative bleeding is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Thromboprophylaxis

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that decisions about peri-operative thromboprophylaxis in NCS are based on individual and procedure-specific risk factors.

If thromboprophylaxis is deemed necessary, it is recommended to choose the type and duration of thromboprophylaxis (LMWH, NOAC, or fondaparinux) according to type of NCS, duration of immobilization, and patient-related factors.
In patients with a low bleeding risk, peri-operative thromboprophylaxis should be considered for a duration of up to 14 or 35 days, for total knee or hip arthroplasty, respectively.
NOACs in thromboprophylaxis dose may be considered as alternative treatments to LMWH after total knee and hip arthroplasty.

recommendation_tables.title: Patient blood management

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to measure haemoglobin pre-operatively in patients scheduled for intermediate- to high-risk NCS.
It is recommended to treat anaemia in advance of NCS in order to reduce the need for RBC transfusion during NCS.
In patients undergoing surgery with expected blood loss of ≥500 mL, use of washed cell salvage is recommended.
It is recommended to use point-of-care diagnostics for guidance of blood component therapy, when available.
The use of an algorithm to diagnose and treat anaemic patients before NCS should be considered.
In patients undergoing NCS and experiencing major bleeding, administration of tranexamic acid should be immediately considered.
Use of closed-loop arterial blood sampling systems should be considered to avoid blood loss.
Application of meticulous haemostasis should be considered a routine procedure.
A feedback/monitoring programme or clinical decision support system should be considered to be assessed before blood transfusion.
Before allogenic blood transfusion, it should be considered to obtain an extensive consent about risks associated with transfusion.

recommendation_tables.title: Coronary artery disease

rows.recommendation: Pre-operative evaluation of patients with an indication for PCI by an expert team (surgeon and cardiologist) should be considered before elective NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Heart failure

rows.recommendation: In patients with HF undergoing NCS, it is recommended to regularly assess volume status and signs of organ perfusion.
A multidisciplinary team including VAD specialists is recommended for peri-operative management of patients with HF receiving mechanical circulatory support.

recommendation_tables.title: Valvular heart disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with symptomatic severe AR or asymptomatic severe AR and LVESD >50 mm or LVESDi (LVESD/BSA) >25 mm/m2 (in patients with small body size) or resting LVEF ≤50%, valve surgery is recommended prior to elective intermediate- or high-risk NCS.
In patients with moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS and symptoms or SPAP >50 mmHg, valve intervention (PMC or surgery) is recommended before elective intermediate- or high-risk NCS.
In asymptomatic patients with severe AS who are scheduled for elective high-risk NCS, AVR (SAVR or TAVI) should be considered after Heart Team discussion.

In patients with symptomatic severe primary MR or asymptomatic severe primary MR with LV dysfunction (LVESD ≥40 mm and/or LVEF ≤60%), valve intervention (surgical or transcatheter) should be considered prior to intermediate- or high-risk NCS, if time allows.

In patients with severe secondary MR who remain symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical therapy (including CRT if indicated), valve intervention (transcatheter or surgical) should be considered before NCS, in eligible patients with an acceptable procedural risk.
In patients with severe symptomatic AS in need of time-sensitive NCS or in whom the TAVI and SAVR are unfeasible, BAV may be considered before NCS as a bridge to definitive aortic valve repair.

recommendation_tables.title: Arrhythmias

rows.recommendation: In AF patients with acute or worsening haemodynamic instability undergoing NCS, emergency electrical cardioversion is recommended.
In patients with symptomatic, monomorphic, sustained VT associated with myocardial scar, recurring despite optimal medical therapy, ablation of arrhythmia is recommended before elective NCS.
It is recommended that all patients with CIEDs that are reprogrammed before surgery have a re-check and necessary reprogramming as soon as possible after the procedure.

If indications for pacing exist according to the 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy, NCS surgery should be deferred and implantation of a permanent pacemaker should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 4B Revised recommendations (2022 version)

rows.recommendation: In patients who have known CVD or CV risk factors (including age ≥65 years), or symptoms or signs suggestive of CVD it is recommended to obtain a pre-operative 12-lead ECG before intermediate- or high-risk NCS.

In patients who have known CVD, CV risk factors (including age ≥65 years), or symptoms suggestive of CVD, it is recommended to measure hs-cTn T or hs-cTn I before intermediate- and high-risk NCS, and at 24 h and 48 h afterwards.
In patients who have known CVD, CV risk factors (including age ≥65 years), or symptoms suggestive of CVD, it should be considered to measure BNP or NT-proBNP before intermediate- and high-risk NCS.
In low-risk patients undergoing low- and intermediate-risk NCS, it is not recommended to routinely obtain pre-operative ECG, hs-cTn T/I, or BNP/NT-proBNP concentrations.
Routine pre-operative ICA is not recommended in stable CCS patients undergoing low- or intermediate-risk NCS.
In patients without HF, withholding RAAS inhibitors on the day of NCS should be considered to prevent peri-operative hypotension.
It is recommended to delay elective NCS until 6 months after elective PCI and 12 months after an ACS.
After elective PCI, it is recommended to delay time-sensitive NCS until a minimum of 1 month of DAPT treatment has been given.
In patients with a previous PCI, it is recommended to continue aspirin peri-operatively if the bleeding risk allows.
In patients without a history of PCI, interruption of aspirin at least 3 days before NCS may be considered if the bleeding risk outweighs the ischaemic risk, to reduce the risk of bleeding.
If interruption of P2Y₁₂ inhibitor is indicated, it is recommended to withhold ticagrelor for 3–5 days, clopidogrel for 5 days, and prasugrel for 7 days prior to NCS.
If PCI is indicated before NCS, the use of new-generation DES is recommended over BMS and balloon angioplasty.

content.title: Recommendations
content.narrative_summary: Section 2.2 The magnitude of the problem discusses the global volume of major surgery, estimated at over 300 million procedures annually (about 5% of the world population), marking a 34% increase from 2004 to 2012. It notes that in Europe, with a 2020 population of 448 million, this translates to roughly 22 million major procedures per year. Nearly 85% of major operations are non-cardiac, and U.S. data indicate that about half of adults aged ≥45 years undergo major non-cardiac surgery.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations

rows.recommendation: Patients with ICDs, whose devices have been pre-operatively deactivated, should be on continuous cardiac monitor throughout the period of deactivation. External defibrillation equipment should be readily available.

It is recommended that patients with temporarily deactivated ICDs have continuous ECG monitoring, and during the peri-operative period are accompanied by personnel skilled in early detection and treatment of arrhythmias. In high-risk patients (e.g. pacemaker-dependent or ICD patients), or if access to the torso will be difficult during the procedure, it is recommended to place transcutaneous pacing/defibrillation pads prior to NCS.
Large peri-operative fluctuations in blood pressure in hypertensive patients should be avoided.

In patients with chronic hypertension undergoing elective NCS, it is recommended to avoid large peri-operative fluctuations in blood pressure, particularly hypotension, during the peri-operative period.
Clinicians may consider not deferring NCS in patients with grade 1 or 2 hypertension (systolic blood pressure <180 mmHg; diastolic blood pressure <110 mmHg).
It is not recommended to defer NCS in patients with stage 1 or 2 hypertension.

Patients with PAD should be clinically assessed for ischaemic heart disease and, if more than two clinical risk factors are present, they should be considered for pre-operative stress or imaging testing.

In patients with poor functional capacity or with significant risk factors or symptoms (such as moderate-to-severe angina pectoris, decompensated HF, valvular disease and significant arrhythmia), referral for cardiac work-up and optimization is recommended prior to elective surgery for PAD or AAA.
In patients at high surgical risk, clinicians should consider screening for elevated HbA1c before major surgery and improving pre-operative glucose control.

In patients with diabetes or disturbed glucose metabolism, a pre-operative HbA1c test is recommended, if this measurement has not been performed in the previous 3 months. In case of HbA1c ≥8.5% (≥69 mmol/mol), elective NCS should be postponed, if safe and practical.
Patients with high cardiac and surgical risk should be considered for goal-directed therapy.
In order to preserve optimal CV stability, it is recommended to apply goal-directed haemodynamic therapy in patients undergoing high-risk NCS.
Avoiding arterial hypotension (mean arterial pressure <60 mmHg) for prolonged cumulative periods (>30 min) may be considered.

In order to minimize the risk of post-operative organ dysfunction, it is recommended to avoid an intra-operative mean arterial pressure decrease of >20% from baseline values or <60–70 mmHg for ≥10 min.
Avoiding non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (especially cyclo-oxygenase-2 inhibitors) as the first-line analgesics in patients with IHD or stroke may be considered.
Non-aspirin NSAIDs are not recommended as first-line analgesics in patients with established or high risk of CVD.

section_headings: 2.5. The outcomes we want to prevent
content.narrative_summary: Section 2.5 outlines the peri-operative cardiovascular outcomes the guidelines aim to prevent, including myocardial infarction, stent thrombosis, heart failure, arrhythmias, pulmonary embolism, ischaemic stroke, and death, and notes the importance of bleeding risk. section_headings: 3.5 Avoidance or allowance for surgery in the individual patient
content.narrative_summary: Section 3.4 discusses the timing of pre-operative cardiovascular risk evaluation, recommending that assessment be performed prior to surgery at the time the decision for non-cardiac surgery (NCS) is made, to provide accurate risk–benefit estimates for informed shared decision-making and to monitor for potential complications. Section 3.5 introduces the challenge of deciding whether cardiovascular disease (CVD) represents a contraindication to NCS, noting that patients with severe heart failure require stabilization before elective procedures but that no definitive list of contraindications exists; this narrative is incomplete on the page. Section 3.6 addresses the patient perspective, emphasizing the need for coordination between surgical and cardiology teams, plain-language communication tailored to patient health literacy, discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives, shared decision-making to support informed consent, management of patient anxiety, and use of educational tools.

rows.recommendation: In patients with a newly detected murmur suggesting clinically significant pathology, TTE is recommended before high-risk NCS.
In patients with a newly detected murmur, but without other signs or symptoms of CVD, TTE should be considered before moderate-risk NCS.
If a patient scheduled for elective NCS has chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of undetected CAD, further diagnostic work-up before NCS is recommended.

content.title: 6.4 Known or newly diagnosed arrhythmias
content.narrative_summary: Arrhythmias pose significant morbidity and mortality risks during non-cardiac surgery. All patients with known tachyarrhythmias should have a 12-lead ECG and cardiology evaluation preoperatively; correction of electrolyte and acid–base imbalances and avoidance of large fluid shifts are essential. Patients on antiarrhythmic drugs should generally continue therapy, with continuous ECG monitoring intra- and post-operatively, and ICDs deactivated during surgery. Supraventricular arrhythmias rarely require surgical deferral; treat SVT with vagal maneuvers, adenosine, beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine CCBs, and consider RF ablation if recurrent. Atrial fibrillation/flutter management includes lifelong oral anticoagulation, rate or rhythm control individualized by hemodynamic status and surgical timing, and choice of pharmacological agents (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, amiodarone, dofetilide or ibutilide) or electrical cardioversion as needed. Premature ventricular contractions and non-sustained VT are common and often benign; in non-cardiac surgery patients without structural disease they require intervention only if frequent or symptomatic.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues guidance on peri-operative management of ventricular arrhythmias, noting that up-titration of beta-blockers is recommended in hemodynamically compromising VT, with amiodarone as an alternative if beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated. Further diagnostics are advised to exclude significant heart disease in patients awaiting non-cardiac surgery, especially those with frequent or complex VT, symptoms, or a family history of sudden cardiac death. Polymorphic VT and VF may result from ischaemia, electrolyte imbalance, or primary electrical disease (e.g., long-QT or Brugada syndrome) and warrant diagnostic work-up to exclude severe ventricular dysfunction and coronary artery disease. Monomorphic VT in structurally normal hearts often has a good prognosis and may be managed conservatively or with beta-blockers, verapamil, sodium channel blockers, or ablation; electrical cardioversion or defibrillation is indicated for unstable VT/VF. Recurrent VT/VF in acute ischaemia can be treated with beta-blockers, amiodarone, or revascularisation. Hemodynamically stable VT may be treated with procainamide, flecainide, or amiodarone if other agents are unavailable.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of contrast-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) in surgical patients, noting that decompensated or chronic heart failure, hypertension, cardio-active drugs, and other non-cardiac triggers increase AKI risk. Contrast-induced AKI is defined by rises in serum creatinine and is often self-limiting, but can lead to overt renal failure. KDIGO guidelines recommend pre-operative isotonic fluid hydration, minimal contrast volume, and use of low- or iso-osmolar agents, with postoperative renal function monitoring via AKI scoring. The section on obesity defines obesity by BMI thresholds, describes the obesity paradox in non-cardiac surgery (lower mortality in mildly obese patients), and suggests cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF, measured by VO₂ max) as a superior CV risk predictor. Cohort studies link good CRF to favourable prognosis, but optimal intervention strategies, including weight loss, remain controversial.

If a cystatin C measurement assay is available, cystatin C measurement should be considered in patients with impaired eGFR (<45–59 mL/min/1.73 m2) to confirm kidney disease.

content.title: Systematic work-up and treatment of peri-operative myocardial injury/infarction
content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses that an absolute increase in cardiac troponin (cTn T/I) above the upper limit of normal (ULN) pre-operatively is linked to higher 30-day and long-term mortality and non-fatal cardiac complications, supporting its use in clinical surveillance for peri-operative myocardial injury (PMI). Evidence suggests benefits of cardiologist-led work-up in reducing mortality. Mortality varies by phenotype, with higher risk in acute heart failure and extra-cardiac PMI. Type 2 MI patients are generally managed as type 1 MI but evidence is limited. A trial of dabigatran 110 mg twice daily in post-operative myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS) showed outcomes with 60% of patients already on aspirin.

Step 2, transthoracic echocardiography to identify other cardiac causes (tachyarrhythmia, acute heart failure, aortic stenosis) and treat. Step 3, evaluate non-cardiac causes (sepsis, pulmonary embolism, stroke) and treat. Step 4, severe anaemia (Hb <80 g/L) or documented hypotension triggers type 2 MI treatment. section_headings: 8.6. Atrial fibrillation and other relevant arrhythmias
content.narrative_summary: This page describes several post-operative cardiovascular complications and their epidemiology, diagnosis, and management principles following major non-cardiac surgery. Section 8.2 reviews the incidence and bleeding risks of spontaneous myocardial infarction occurring after day 2, noting rates of ≈0.5% within 30 days and 1–2% within 365 days and recommending management per specialty MI guidelines. Section 8.3 discusses the detection of Takotsubo syndrome via peri-operative TTE and its likely under-recognition. Section 8.4 summarizes the incidence of post-operative acute heart failure (1–2% at 30 days, 4–6% at 365 days) and the importance of diagnostic work-up and therapy. Section 8.5 highlights the uncertain incidence of peri-operative venous thromboembolism, risk factors, and the need for appropriate screening. Section 8.6 outlines the epidemiology of new-onset post-operative atrial fibrillation (2–30% incidence, peak at 2–4 days) and its association with adverse outcomes. Subsection 8.6.1 reviews pharmacologic prevention of post-operative AF, noting the protective effects of pre-operative beta-blockers, mixed evidence for peri-operative metoprolol, and amiodarone dosing strategies.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative notes that evidence for interventions such as statins, magnesium, sotalol, colchicine, or corticosteroids in post-operative AF is not robust. In haemodynamically unstable patients with post-operative AF, emergent electrical or pharmacological cardioversion (e.g., i.v. amiodarone or vernakalant) is indicated. In stable patients, optimal ventricular rate control using beta-blockers or verapamil is mandatory, and non-emergent cardioversion may be avoided. For AF lasting ≥48 hours, cardioversion should follow pericardioversion thromboprophylaxis, either performed only after exclusion of left atrial thrombus or postponed for three weeks of therapeutic OAC.

content.narrative_summary: Section 8.6.2.2 discusses initiation of therapeutic anticoagulation as soon as possible in all patients with post-operative atrial fibrillation, based on individual stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) and bleeding risk. Observational data show higher short- and long-term stroke and mortality risks in post-operative AF, and long-term OAC (LMWH, fondaparinux, non-vitamin K antagonist OACs preferred over VKAs) is recommended, with re-evaluation after 3 months. Section 8.7 reviews peri-operative stroke incidence across surgical types (0.08–3%) and associated mortality, highlighting ischaemic and cardioembolic mechanisms, hypoperfusion, embolism, and the need for immediate imaging and intervention.

It is recommended to treat post-operative STEMI, NSTE-ACS, acute HF, and tachyarrhythmias in accordance with guidelines for the non-surgical setting, after interdisciplinary discussion with the surgeon about bleeding risk.

In patients with post-operative PE of high or intermediate clinical probability, initiation of anticoagulation is recommended without delay, while diagnostic work-up is in progress, if bleeding risk is low.

In patients with a post-operative indication for OAC, NOAC is generally recommended over VKA.

In patients with post-operative AF after NCS, long-term OAC therapy should be considered in all patients at risk of stroke, considering the anticipated net clinical benefit of OAC therapy, and informed patient preferences.
In patients with MINS and at low risk of bleeding, treatment with dabigatran 110 mg orally b.i.d. may be considered from ∼1 week after NCS.

section_headings: 12. ‘What to do’ and ‘what not to do’ messages from the Guidelines
content.narrative_summary: Section 11 discusses how sex and gender influence management and outcomes in non-cardiac surgery (NCS). It notes that women have a lower age-adjusted incidence of cardiovascular disease but may face undetected disease and higher post-operative mortality in certain subgroups, such as those with heart failure. Data on sex-specific strategies are lacking. Women have higher rates of anaemia, lower blood volumes, and haemoglobin levels leading to more post-operative complications and transfusions, underscoring the need for tailored blood-management programs. Physiological and pharmacokinetic differences may affect anaesthesia, pain management, recovery, and satisfaction. Sex differences have been reported in patients undergoing cardiac device implantation and in stroke risk among those with atrial fibrillation, but specific outcome data for device or arrhythmia patients undergoing NCS are limited.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for clinical risk evaluation

rows.recommendation: In all patients scheduled for NCS, an accurate history and clinical examination are recommended.
It is recommended to perform a pre-operative risk assessment, ideally at the same time as the NCS is proposed.
If time allows, it is recommended to optimize guideline-recommended treatment of CVD and CV risk factors before NCS.
In patients with a family history of genetic cardiomyopathy, it is recommended to perform an ECG and TTE before NCS, regardless of age and symptoms.
In patients with a newly detected murmur and symptoms or signs of CVD, TTE is recommended before NCS.
In patients with a newly detected murmur suggesting clinically significant pathology, TTE is recommended before high-risk NCS.

section_headings: Recommendations for patient blood management in NCS
Recommendations for management of patients with specific diseases undergoing NCS
content.narrative_summary: This page presents ESC guideline recommendations for peri-operative management in non-cardiac surgery (NCS). It covers antiplatelet therapy management, interruption and bridging of oral anticoagulants, peri-operative thromboprophylaxis, patient blood management, and specific recommendations for patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and heart failure (HF), each with assigned Class of Recommendation and Level of Evidence.

rows.recommendation: In patients with a previous PCI, it is recommended to continue aspirin peri-operatively if the bleeding risk allows.
If interruption of P2Y12 inhibitor is indicated, it is recommended to withhold ticagrelor for 3–5 days, clopidogrel for 5 days, and prasugrel for 7 days prior to NCS.
For patients undergoing high bleeding risk surgery (e.g. intracranial, spinal neurosurgery, or vitreoretinal eye surgery), it is recommended to interrupt aspirin for at least 7 days pre-operatively.

If antiplatelet therapy has been interrupted before a surgical procedure, it is recommended to restart therapy as soon as possible (within 48 h) post-surgery, according to interdisciplinary risk assessment.
When an urgent surgical intervention is required, it is recommended that NOAC therapy is immediately interrupted.
In minor bleeding risk surgery and other procedures where bleeding can easily be controlled, it is recommended to perform surgery without interruption of OAC therapy.
In non-minor bleeding risk procedures in patients using a NOAC, it is recommended to use an interruption regimen based on the NOAC compound, renal function, and bleeding risk.
In patients using NOACs, it is recommended that minor bleeding risk procedures are performed at trough levels (typically 12–24 h after last intake).
LMWH is recommended, as an alternative to UFH, for bridging in patients with MHVs and high surgical risk.
Bridging of OAC therapy is not recommended in patients with low/moderate thrombotic risk undergoing NCS.
Use of reduced-dose NOAC to attenuate the risk of post-operative bleeding is not recommended.
It is recommended that decisions about peri-operative thromboprophylaxis in NCS are based on individual and procedure-specific risk factors.

If thromboprophylaxis is deemed necessary, it is recommended to choose the type and duration of thromboprophylaxis (LMWH, NOAC, or fondaparinux) according to type of NCS, duration of immobilization, and patient-related factors.
It is recommended to measure haemoglobin pre-operatively in patients scheduled for intermediate- to high-risk NCS.
It is recommended to treat anaemia in advance of NCS in order to reduce the need for RBC transfusion during NCS.
In patients undergoing surgery with expected blood loss of ≥500 mL, use of washed cell salvage is recommended.
It is recommended to use point-of-care diagnostics for guidance of blood component therapy, when available.
If PCI is indicated before NCS, the use of new-generation DES is recommended over BMS and balloon angioplasty.

If NCS can safely be postponed (e.g. at least 3 months), it is recommended that patients with ACS being scheduled for NCS undergo diagnostic and therapeutic interventions as recommended for ACS patients in general.
Routine myocardial revascularization before low- and intermediate-risk NCS in patients with CCS is not recommended.

In patients with suspected or known HF scheduled for high-risk NCS, it is recommended to evaluate LV function with echocardiography and measurement of NT-proBNP/BNP levels, unless this has recently been performed.
It is recommended that patients with HF undergoing NCS receive optimal medical treatment according to current ESC Guidelines.
In patients with HF undergoing NCS, it is recommended to regularly assess volume status and signs of organ perfusion.

recommendation_tables.title: Patients with VHD

rows.recommendation: Clinical and echocardiographic evaluation (if not recently performed) is recommended in all patients with known or suspected VHD who are scheduled for elective intermediate- or high-risk NCS.
AVR (SAVR or TAVI) is recommended in symptomatic patients with severe AS who are scheduled for elective intermediate- or high-risk NCS.

In patients with symptomatic severe AR or asymptomatic severe AR and LVESD >50 mm or LVESDi (LVESD/BSA) >25 mm/m2 (in patients with small body size) or resting LVEF <50%, valve surgery is recommended prior to elective intermediate- or high-risk NCS.

In patients with moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS and symptoms or SPAP >50 mmHg, valve intervention (percutaneous mitral commissurotomy or surgery) is recommended before elective intermediate- or high-risk NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Patients with ACHD

rows.recommendation: In patients with ACHD, a consultation with an ACHD specialist is recommended before intermediate- or high-risk surgery.
In patients with ACHD, it is recommended that intermediate- and high-risk elective surgery is performed in a centre with experience in the care of ACHD patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Patients with arrhythmias

rows.recommendation: In patients with SVT controlled by medication, it is recommended that AADs are continued during the peri-operative period.
In AF patients with acute or worsening haemodynamic instability undergoing NCS, emergency electrical cardioversion is recommended.
In patients with symptomatic, monomorphic, and sustained VT associated with myocardial scar, recurring despite optimal medical therapy, ablation of arrhythmia is recommended before elective NCS.

It is recommended that patients with temporarily deactivated ICDs have continuous ECG monitoring, and during the peri-operative period are accompanied by personnel skilled in early detection and treatment of arrhythmias. In high-risk patients (e.g. pacemaker-dependant or ICD patients), or if access to the torso will be difficult during the procedure, it is recommended to place transcutaneous pacing/defibrillation pads prior to NCS.
It is recommended that all patients with CIEDs that are reprogrammed before surgery have a re-check and necessary reprogramming as soon as possible after the procedure.
It is not recommended to initiate treatment of asymptomatic PVC during NCS.

recommendation_tables.title: Patients with pulmonary hypertension

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to continue chronic therapy for PAH in the peri-operative phase of NCS.
It is recommended that haemodynamic monitoring of patients with severe PAH continues for at least 24 h in the post-operative period.

In the case of progression of right HF in the post-operative period in patients with PAH, it is recommended that the diuretic dose be optimized and, if necessary, i.v. prostacyclin analogues be initiated under the guidance of a physician experienced in the management of PAH.

recommendation_tables.title: Patients with hypertension

rows.recommendation: In patients with chronic hypertension undergoing elective NCS, it is recommended to avoid large peri-operative fluctuations in blood pressure, particularly hypotension, during the peri-operative period.
It is recommended to perform pre-operative screening for hypertension-mediated organ damage and CV risk factors in newly diagnosed hypertensive patients who are scheduled for elective high-risk NCS.
It is not recommended to defer NCS in patients with stage 1 or 2 hypertension.

recommendation_tables.title: Patients with PAD

rows.recommendation: In patients with poor functional capacity or with significant risk factors or symptoms (such as moderate-to-severe angina pectoris, decompensated HF, valvular disease and significant arrhythmia), referral for cardiac work-up and optimization is recommended prior to elective surgery for PAD or AAA.
Routine referral for cardiac work-up, coronary angiography, or CPET prior to elective surgery for PAD or AAA is not recommended.

section_headings: Recommendations for peri-operative monitoring and anaesthesia
Recommendations for treatment of post-operative cardiovascular complications
content.narrative_summary: This page presents recommendations for pre-operative assessment and imaging in patients with cerebrovascular disease, renal disease, obesity, and diabetes, followed by guidance on peri-operative hemodynamic management, pain control, and treatment of post-operative cardiovascular complications including myocardial injury, STEMI, NSTE-ACS, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, and atrial fibrillation.

rows.recommendation: Pre-operative carotid artery and cerebral imaging is recommended in patients with a history of TIA or stroke in the previous 6 months and who have not undergone ipsilateral revascularization.
Pre-operative routine carotid artery imaging is not recommended in patients undergoing NCS.

In patients with known risk factors (age >65 years, BMI >30 kg/m2, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, CV disease, or smoking) undergoing intermediate- or high-risk NCS, it is recommended to screen for pre-operative renal disease by measuring serum creatinine and GFR.
It is recommended to assess cardiorespiratory fitness to estimate peri-operative CV risk in obese patients, with particular attention to those undergoing intermediate- and high-risk NCS.

A pre-operative assessment for concomitant cardiac conditions is recommended in patients with diabetes with suspected or known CAD, and those with autonomic neuropathy, retinopathy, or renal disease and scheduled to undergo intermediate- and high-risk NCS.

In patients with diabetes or disturbed glucose metabolism, a pre-operative HbA1c is recommended, if this measurement has been not performed in the previous 3 months. In case of HbA1c ≥8.5% (≥69 mmol/mol), elective NCS should be postponed, if safe and practical.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for peri-operative monitoring and anaesthesia

rows.recommendation: In order to preserve optimal CV stability, it is recommended to apply goal-directed haemodynamic therapy in patients undergoing high-risk NCS.
It is recommended to avoid post-operative acute pain.

In order to minimize the risk of post-operative organ dysfunction, it is recommended to avoid an intra-operative mean arterial pressure decrease of >20% from baseline values or <60–70 mmHg for ≥10 min.
Non-aspirin NSAIDs are not recommended as first-line analgesics in patients with established or high risk of CVD.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for treatment of post-operative cardiovascular complications

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to have high awareness of peri-operative CV complications, combined with surveillance for PMI in patients undergoing intermediate- or high-risk NCS.
Systematic PMI work-up is recommended to identify the underlying pathophysiology and define therapy.

It is recommended to treat post-operative STEMI, NSTE-ACS, acute HF, and tachyarrhythmias in accordance with guidelines for the non-surgical setting, after interdisciplinary discussion with the surgeon about bleeding risk.

In patients with post-operative PE of high or intermediate clinical probability, initiation of anticoagulation is recommended without delay, while diagnostic work-up is in progress, if bleeding risk is low.
Post-operative oral anticoagulation for PE is recommended to be administered for a period of at least 3 months.
In patients with a post-operative indication for OAC, NOAC is generally recommended over VKA.
Routine use of beta-blocker for the prevention of post-operative AF in patients undergoing NCS is not recommended.

content.narrative_summary: Section 13 introduces quality indicators (QIs) as tools to evaluate and enhance care quality for cardiovascular disease, describes the ESC’s development and embedding of QI suites in recent guidelines, and outlines integration with registries (EUROObservational Research Programme, European Unified Registries On Heart Care Evaluation and Randomized Trials) and the EuroHeart project. It notes a parallel process to develop QIs for non-cardiac surgery (NCS) patients, to be published separately. Section 14 explains that peri-operative cardiovascular risk depends on both intrinsic surgical risk and patient factors, requiring multidisciplinary cooperation (see Figure 21).
